bib.title: DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database
bib.venue: SIGMOD '19 (International Conference on Management of Data), demonstration track

question: How can an analytical (OLAP) SQL database be built to run embedded inside a host process, as SQLite does for transactional workloads?
hypothesis: An embeddable, purpose-built analytical engine will keep working on larger data on restricted hardware, where SQLite, MonetDBLite and HyPer degrade (stated as an expectation for the demo, not tested).
contributions: DuckDB, a new purpose-built embeddable relational DBMS for analytics, MIT licensed
A demonstration comparing DuckDB with SQLite, MonetDBLite and HyPer on small devices as data size grows

method.summary: The paper describes DuckDB's architecture: Postgres-derived parser, binder and logical planner, cost-based optimizer, vectorized interpreted execution, serializable MVCC and DataBlocks storage, reached through a C/C++ API with a SQLite compatibility layer. It then plans a live demo with four benchmark computers loaded with TPC-H. No experiment has been run or reported.
method.task: embeddable analytical database design and demonstration

datasets.name: TPC-H tables
datasets.source: TPC-H benchmark, pre-loaded on each of four computers

other.optimizer: cost-based; dynamic programming join ordering with greedy fallback; subquery flattening per Neumann and Kemper
other.execution: vectorized, 'Vector Volcano' chunk pulling, 1024 values per vector by default
other.storage: DataBlocks with light-weight compression, per-column min/max indexes (planned, not complete)
other.api: C/C++, SQLite compatibility layer, R DBI, Python PEP 249

other.demo_hardware: four identical 'benchmark computers' (specs not given) plus a fifth management computer, Ethernet
other.demo_scenarios: 'teaser' (pre-configured query, audience turns dial for input size) and 'drilldown' (audience proposes query)

metrics.name: QpS
metrics.definition: query completion rate, shown live for each system

metrics.name: memory pressure
metrics.definition: real-time memory metric per system, not further defined

eval.protocol: Live demo; one query repeated on all four machines while a dial scales the share of fact-table data read. No runs, seeds or results are reported.

results.claim: The default vector holds 1024 values in DuckDB's vectorized interpreted engine.
results.setup: Design description and demo plan only; no measurements are reported in the paper; a design parameter, not a result
results.quote: DuckDB uses vectors of a fixed maximum amount of values (1024 per default).

results.claim: SQLite is called the most widely deployed SQL engine, with more than a trillion databases in active use, but its row-major B-tree engine performs very poorly on OLAP.
results.setup: Assertion with no benchmark in this paper; trillion figure is cited to SQLite docs [4]
results.quote: SQLite strongly focuses on transactional (OLTP) workloads, and con- tains a row-major execution engine operating on a B-Tree storage format [3]. As a consequence, SQLite’s performance on analytical (OLAP) workloads is very poor.

results.claim: At the time of writing DuckDB runs all TPC-H queries and all but two TPC-DS queries.
results.quote: As of this writing, DuckDB runs all TPC-H queries and all but two TPC-DS queries.

results.claim: DuckDB chose a vectorized interpreted engine over JIT compilation for portability, since JIT engines depend on large compiler libraries such as LLVM.
results.quote: This approach was chosen over Just-in-Time compilation (JIT) of SQL queries [8] for portability reasons.

results.claim: The authors expect the demo to show only DuckDB still functioning at larger dataset sizes, while the others degrade; this is a prediction, not a measured outcome.
results.setup: Demo of SQLite, MonetDBLite, HyPer, DuckDB on four identical computers, TPC-H tables, a dial controlling input size; future tense, nothing run yet
results.quote: While for very small data sets all systems will show com- parable behavior, only DuckDB will be able to continue func- tioning for larger ones.

results.claim: DuckDB used HyPer's serializable MVCC, updating in place with an undo buffer, chosen over optimistic concurrency control because parallel table modification was often requested.
results.quote: This variant updates data in-place immediately, and keeps previous states stored in a separate undo buffer for concurrent transactions and aborts.

results.claim: In 2019 DuckDB lacked a finished DataBlocks storage scheme, cardinality estimation, a buffer manager and intra-query parallelism.
results.setup: State of the system at paper time; later releases have dated this
results.quote: Immediate next steps for DuckDB are completion of Dat- aBlocks storage scheme and cardinality estimating. A buffer manager is also not yet implemented, but will be.

limits: No experiment or measurement is reported; the demonstration is described in the future tense, so no performance claim is backed by data.
Hardware, TPC-H scale factor, queries and data sizes for the demo are not given.
Authors concede in 2019 that DataBlocks storage, cardinality estimation, a buffer manager and intra-query parallelism were unfinished, and TPC-DS coverage was two queries short.
Says nothing about file formats such as Parquet, CSV or object stores.
Dated: the system described is the 2019 prototype; later DuckDB releases differ.
